newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Act NZ to vote against National's Maori land bill.
newsitem.headline: Act NZ to vote against National's Maori land bill.

text.p: Act New Zealand will not ratify the government's recent deal with the South Island's Ngai Tahu tribe if New Zealanders' property rights are sacrificed, leader Richard Prebble said on Tuesday.

Act has backed National's economic policies and is a potential coalition partner if National can return to power after the October 12 general election. However, Prebble described the government's moves to settle Treaty of Waitangi Maori claims as "outrageous".
Speaking in Auroa in Taranaki, he said Act would vote against the National party's Maori Reserve Land Amendment Bill in its present form.

On Friday, after five years of negotiation, the government agreed in principle with Ngai Tahu Maori to settle the tribe's claim to large tracts of the South Island. Under the settlement, the government will give Ngai Tahu a formal apology and NZ$170 million in land and cash.
Prebble said National's handling of Maori land claims had "gone off the rails".
The bill, presently before parliament, offered inadequate compensation to private land owners whose land is under Maori claim, Prebble said.

Many farmers hold their land in perpetual leases, a property right recognised by the court. Prebble said the bill proposed to change the leases to seven year rent reviews, and to strip lessees of the right to sell their land to whoever they chose.
"The bill offers the lessees inadequate compensation... In plain English, the government is proposing stealing private property from about 600 families to settle a Waitangi Treaty claim," he said.

"Act MPs give you this assurance that we will not only vote against the bill in its present form but we will shame parliament into giving you all fair and adequate compensation," Prebble told Taranaki farmers.

Prebble said Act recognised that Taranaki Maori had real grievances which needed to be resolved, but said if the government had determined it owed Maori a settlement then the government, not a few individuals, must pay.

He also said that with the Ngai Tahu deal the government had broken a constitutional convention which stated that after parliament was prorogued no action should be taken that required a subsequent parliament's approval.

The Ngai Tahu tribe's grievances date back to 1844 when the colonial authorities bought the first of 10 parcels of land covering most of the South Island for what it now acknowledges was an artificially low price.
Colonial powers went on to acquire 34 million hectares (84 million acres), most of the South Island, for just 14,750 pounds. Promises to create reserve lands for Maori were never honoured.
The government has set aside NZ$1 billion to settle all Maori claims.
